source_title: Live: Appeal decision due shortly for triple murderer Erin Patterson
source_excerpt:
Victoria's highest court has increased Erin Patterson's jail term to life in prison without parole and dismissed an appeal against her murder convictions.
Read back on how the court proceeding unfolded in our blog.
Choose what information you see below by using filters
Thank you so much for joining us for today's coverage of Erin Patterson's appeal decision.
To keep up with our coverage and any fresh developments, check out our story below:
WATCH: Victoria's Court of Appeal hands down Erin Patterson judgment
Justice Stephen McLeish dismissed Erin Patterson's appeal against her murder convictions and resentenced the killer to life in prison without parole.
Are there many other murderers who gets real life sentences?
ABC court reporter Kristian Silva mentioned today that this new, harsher sentence is very rare in Australia.
"There are not many killers in Australia that have got a life sentence without parole. This is the worst of the worst," Silva said.
"There’s only a handful in the country. We’re talking the likes of Martin Bryant — that is the level that Erin Patterson now finds herself at."
Who instigated the appeal? I understand both sides appealed but did one go first?
The prosecution got their paperwork in first, but the defence indicated pretty early on that they would be appealing.
Prosecutors were always going to call for a harsher sentence
If Erin had not lodged an appeal, would the prosecution still have lodged theirs?
The answer is yes, because the appeals were on separate issues.
After Patterson was found guilty, the prosecution always called for her to be jailed for life with no parole due to the seriousness of the crime.
WATCH: Recapping the Court of Appeal decision
The ABC's Alexandra Alvaro and Kristian Silva are outside the Court of Appeal. They are taking us through what occurred today and what is ahead for Erin Patterson.
Erin Patterson has become headline news in recent years, known as the infamous murderous cook behind a mushroom meal that killed three relatives.
But Patterson, born Erin Scutter, divided opinions even before her murder trial, with former colleagues recalling a "crafty" air traffic controller with a tendency to snap and "say something unpleasant at the drop of a hat".
To learn more about the woman behind the murders, read our story below.
Who is paying all the legal costs for these appeals?
I have a procedural question. I'm wondering how Erin Patterson has funded her legal representation for the trial and appeal. The amounts involved must have been significant. Did she receive legal aid? Did she fund them herself? Did the court decide to grant her funding assistance given the nature and seriousness of the charges against her?
While we don't have a detailed view of Erin Patterson's finances, there are a few things we do know.
Patterson's lawyers are listed as a mortgagee on the Leongatha home where she hosted the deadly lunch.
She had moved into the home with her children in 2022. She told the court she saw it as the home she would live in for the rest of her life.
But a Supreme Court order in 2025 barred her from selling the home because it would likely need to be sold to pay for compensation claims.
As for her other assets, we know Patterson has been the beneficiary of two inheritances, one from her grandmother and the other from her own mother.
When her grandmother died in 2006, Patterson received $2 million , distributed to her over several years.
During her murder trial, the court heard Patterson used her wealth to issue interest-free loans to Simon Patterson's siblings so they could purchase properties of their own.
Reporter Sacha Payne was in the Supreme Court building as the judgment was handed down:
Erin Patterson was not in court for today’s decision, appearing only as a small figure at the bottom of a large screen beaming her image into the Court of Appeal from the Dame Phyllis Frost Centre, where she is serving her life sentence.
She was impassive as the judge explained his reasons, appearing to close her eyes at some points.
The room was silent as reporters, members of the public and lawyers listened to the judge.
There was an intake of breath when the room learnt the prosecution’s appeal against her sentence was successful, removing her non-parole period.
Outside the court, prosecutors, police investigators and supporters of Erin’s ex-husband Simon Patterson grinned broadly.
Erin seems to have protection and privileges in prison, will these continue?
Will this change how she is housed within the correction centre at all or will that be unchanged?
Is it likely that Erin Patterson will remain in isolation in prison?
Erin Patterson's day-to-day life in prison featured heavily in both her sentencing and appeal hearings.
As you note, she is currently kept in the maximum-security Gordon Unit for her own protection, given her role in one of Victoria's most high-profile murder cases.
Both prosecutors and her lawyers agreed she was likely to be kept in solitary confinement in this unit for "years to come".
In terms of privileges, the court has previously heard she has access to a small exercise yard and treadmill, as well as a library, but she has to request access to these services.
However, it was raised to the court that due to the resourcing issues at the Dame Phyllis Frost Centre, these services weren't always available and she was forced to spend the majority of her time in her cell. It was also mentioned she is a keen crocheter in her cell.
Whether her notoriety diminishes and these restrictions are relaxed in the years and decades to come is still unknown.
Erin Patterson appeared emotionless as fate was sealed
What was Erin Patterson's reaction to the decision?
The ABC's Jarrod Whittaker was covering today's hearing. He said Erin Patterson showed no emotion when Justice McLeish handed down the decision.
While she shed tears and was emotional at times during her murder trial, she was reserved during the appeals process, seen only occasionally shaking her head as prosecutors made their arguments.
Why did Erin Patterson receive a harsher sentence?
How is it that Erin Patterson's sentence can be changed after an appeal?
There were actually two appeals decided today. One from Erin Patterson trying to clear her name, and one from Crown prosecutors who said the initial 33-year sentence she received wasn't strong enough.
The prosecutors argued that, given the amount of planning, her ties to her relatives and the fact she had shown no remorse since the fatal lunch, she didn't deserve a chance at freedom.
The Court of Appeal judges agreed with the prosecution's argument, increasing her sentence.
What is the legal test that would need to be satisfied for her to appeal to the High Court of Australia?
Crown prosecutors have successfully argued that Erin Patterson's crimes are so serious that she should never have a chance at freedom.
It means Patterson is looking at spending the rest of her life in prison.
The convicted murderer now has very few options available to her, and some very steep legal hurdles to climb if she even wants a chance to appeal.
Reforms were introduced in 2019 that would allow for a second appeal if fresh and compelling evidence came to light exonerating her, but legal experts we have spoken to have stressed this is a very rare occurrence.
Patterson could also take her case to the High Court of Australia, but in doing so she would have clear a very high bar of legal argument.
It is only very rarely a possibility, as in the case of Cardinal George Pell in 2020.
For more on her options, you can check out our explainer below:
Leave to appeal is granted against ground one and two only, but the appeal is dismissed. What does it mean appeal is granted but the appeal is dismissed?
Why is it that an appeal can be granted and also dismissed?
It is a little confusing, but you must first convince the Court of Appeal that your argument has merit before they'll decide to actually deeply consider the legal ramifications of your complaint.
Erin Patterson's lawyers brought seven different reasons they believed there was a miscarriage of justice.
The Court of Appeal judges said they would only grant leave to appeal for the first two , and dismissed the other five (things like the lead prosecutor being unfair with her questioning) outright.
They then considered the first two grounds, which were:
The mistake that occurred with the jury staying in the same hotel as a police witness
The use of Patterson's mobile phone data as evidence
The judges considered these two grounds, but decided there were no issues and dismissed them because they were not convinced.
What today's decision means is that Erin Patterson will no longer be eligible for parole in 33 years. Instead, she will spend the rest of her life behind bars.
In terms of her future, she is left with very few legal avenues. Other than the rare case of new evidence exonerating Patterson, her only option would be to appeal against this decision in the High Court of Australia.
But legal experts say there is an extremely high legal bar for Patterson to clear in order for her to be able to appeal to the High Court.
Justice McLeish says the non-parole period will be set aside, and that the prosecution's appeal for a harsher sentence is successful.
He says Patterson's conduct deserves to be "denounced in the strongest terms", and it is inappropriate for parole to be an option.
Justice McLeish says offending was severe
Justice McLeish says Erin Patterson's conduct was characterised by "an elaborate series of deceptions".
He raises the false cancer claim, the destruction of evidence, the planning of the lunch and the "cruel breach of trust" of her relatives.
Leave to appeal granted, appeal dismissed
Leave to appeal is granted against ground one and two only, but the appeal is dismissed.
Justice McLeish says the second ground — the evidence of mobile phone data — is also unsuccessful.
Justice McLeish is recapping what occurred during the appeals process, and the seven grounds on which Patterson is appealing.
He says the first ground is unsuccessful be there is no possibility the jury would not have made a correct decision even after being accommodated in the same hotel as a police witness.
Justice Stephen McLeish, Justice Lesley Taylor and Justice Peter Kidd are now delivering their decision on Erin Patterson's appeal.
Erin Patterson has chosen not to come to court in person today, and will watch proceedings from the Dame Phyllis Frost women's prison.
She is being beamed into the courtroom and can be seen sitting in a white room, staring out a large window to her right.
Lawyers, journalists and members of the public are filling the seats of courtroom 1 of the Supreme Court, which has just opened.
Members of Victoria Police's Homicide Squad are here, and some members of the extended Patterson and Wilkinson family.
Victoria's Director of Public Prosecutions appealed on the basis that the sentence handed down to Patterson was "manifestly inadequate".
Patterson was sentenced to life in prison with a 33-year non-parole period over the murders of relatives Don and Gail Patterson and Heather Wilkinson.
She was also convicted of the attempted murder of Heather's husband Ian Wilkinson, who survived the lunch but spent weeks recovering in hospital.
Patterson was spared the harshest penalty under the law — a life sentence with no parole — meaning with time already served she could be freed in 2056.
The judge who handed down the sentence, Justice Beale, said he had given Patterson the chance for parole due to her harsher-than-usual prison conditions, which included being housed in a small cell in solitary confinement.
However, prosecutors argued this was an "error" by the judge because Corrections Victoria staff reviewed Patterson's conditions on a monthly basis.
They also argued Patterson remained remorseless over her actions and that her crimes fell into the "worst category".
You can read more about the prosecution's appeal here:
Even though it's a massive day for Patterson as she tries to have her convictions overturned, she is not expected to be in court today.
It's understood she will watch the court proceedings online from the Dame Phillis Frost Centre where she is serving time.
During both her sentencing and her appeal, Erin Patterson's lawyers told the court about her living conditions in prison, which they said were extremely challenging.
Her defence team said Patterson was forced to spend between 22 and 24 hours alone in a maximum security wing away from other prisoners due to her notoriety. They argued this constituted solitary confinement, as defined by the United Nations.
The court heard Patterson had little access to fresh air, had food delivered through a trap door, and only had permission to communicate with one other prisoner, who was a convicted terrorist.
Her lawyers said her confinement meant her prison term was all the more punishing, and meant her jail sentence was adequate.
Prosecutors disagreed, arguing Patterson's notoriety would eventually fade over time, and that she still had access to services such as a library and a chaplain.
Revisiting the sentencing of Erin Patterson
Erin Patterson was sentenced in September last year in the culmination of a court case that had gripped Australia for two years.
Justice Christopher Beale said during his 46-minute sentencing that it was clear Erin Patterson was guilty of the worst kind of offending.
He gave Patterson three life sentences for the murders of Don and Gail Patterson as well as Heather Wilkinson, and 25 years for the attempted murder of Ian Wilkinson.
Justice Beale ruled the severity of her crimes was such that Erin Patterson must remain incarcerated for at least 33 years before parole could be considered.
You can read about his considerations in determining Patterson's sentence here:
If you'd like to watch the decision being handed down yourself, the Supreme Court website has this link for the public to watch.
What time is the judgement expected- morning or afternoon?
We're expecting the Court of Appeal to hand down its decision at 10am AEDT.
We'll bring it to you moment by moment here on the blog.
What are the potential outcomes of today's judgments?
The three Court of Appeal judges are handing down judgments on two appeals today:
1) Erin Patterson's appeal against her convictions
2) The prosecution's appeal against her sentence
The judgment on Patterson's appeal against her convictions will be handed down first as the outcome could mean that a decision on the prosecution's appeal is not required.
The judges are ruling first on whether she can actually lodge an appeal and, if that is granted, on the outcome of any appeal.
That means there are four potential outcomes for her conviction appeal . The judges could rule:
b) Leave to appeal granted, appeal dismissed
c) Leave to appeal granted, appeal upheld, retrial ordered
d) Leave to appeal granted, appeal upheld, acquittal entered
Should the judges hand down a judgment of c] or d], the sentence appeal will not be required.
For the sentence appeal , there are two potential outcomes:
a) The appeal is dismissed and the initial life sentence with a non-parole period of 33 years remains
b) The appeal is upheld and she is resentenced by the Court of Appeal
What was the basis for Erin Patterson's appeal?
The primary argument put forward by Erin Patterson's lawyers was that the verdicts in her triple-murder trial were compromised by a "catastrophic" jury accommodation arrangement.
Her legal team's argument centred on how the jurors considered their verdicts while housed in the same accommodation as the case's lead homicide detective and some prosecutors.
Her barrister, Richard Edney, argued this went against the notion that justice needed to be done, as well as being seen to be done in "perhaps one of the most high-profile criminal trials this state has ever had".
However, under questioning from Court of Appeal judges Lesley Taylor, Stephen McLeish and Peter Kidd, Mr Edney conceded there was no evidence police or prosecutors directly communicated with jurors.

We'll be bringing you all the developments this morning as Erin Patterson learns the outcome of her appeal against her murder convictions.
